title: The New Trustees
author: Aaron Renn
summary: Aaron Renn argues that with the collapse of institutional trust—in journalism, academia, and the professions—Americans are now self-appointing individual 'trustees': public intellectuals they personally select and hold to fiduciary standards. This makes individual public intellectuals structural elements in society, supplying support columns that disappeared with institutional decline. Renn identifies eight attributes of these 'New Trustees': genuine pursuit of truth, constructive insight with owned frameworks, moral seriousness without moralizing, class-traitor courage, non-pandering to their own audiences, generosity of spirit, being defined by what they are for rather than against, and even temperament. He distinguishes them from 'false friends'—people with moderate demeanor but little genuine insight, whose apparent courage is usually inter-factional. The recurring diagnostic: once someone becomes an 'anti'—organized primarily by opposition—their insight generation collapses.
points: With institutional trust collapsed, Americans now self-appoint individual trustees—public intellectuals they personally select and hold to fiduciary standards of loyalty, care, and good faith.

The New Trustee's most distinguishing feature is a felt fiduciary responsibility to the truth and to the people who've placed trust in them—not just being trustworthy, but actively serving the beneficiary.
Class-traitor courage distinguishes New Trustees from false friends: they are willing to say difficult things that cost them money or status among people whose opinion genuinely matters to them.
New Trustees are not antis—they are defined by what they are for, not what they oppose. Once someone becomes an anti, the amount of insight they generate collapses.

False friends have moderate demeanor and apparent courage, but their criticism is usually directed at rival factions rather than their actual peer group—a structurally different act requiring far less courage.
quotes: trust has been devolved. People no longer have a default in trust institutions; they trust and follow individuals they’ve personally selected.
But they are supplying important support columns that disappeared with the decline of institutions in America.
A trustee has a fiduciary responsibility to the beneficiary and must act in the beneficiary’s interest.
perhaps the most distinguishing feature of the New Trustees is that they feel a fiduciary responsibility to the truth, and to the people who’ve placed trust in them to provide it.
once someone becomes an “anti,” the amount of insight they generate plummets. You can almost see the light bulb turning off.
They write (or publish) serious works for serious people who are also interested in getting it right and don’t mind being challenged from time to time.
